summary: Explains why the IAB believes that, when the interests of end users conflict with those of other parties, IETF decisions should favor end users. It also explores how the IETF can more effectively achieve this. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The people who design the Internet's rules should think first of the ordinary people using it. This document explains why and gives ideas on how to put users first when their interests clash with others'.

questions: why is the internet for end users
what does the iab say about end users
how should the ietf make decisions about standards
subtitle: Why the Internet's technical standards should prioritize ordinary users

tldr.problem: Technical standards for the Internet affect many parties: vendors, operators, content owners, governments, and end users. When these interests conflict, it is unclear whose needs should win.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Architecture Board argues that IETF decisions should favor end users—the humans whose activities the protocols ultimately support—over the interests of other stakeholders.
tldr.outcome: The IETF can better achieve its mission to build a better human society by prioritizing end users: engaging the Internet community, designing user-focused systems, identifying negative impacts, and avoiding internal convenience at the cost of user harm.

today: RFC 8890 is an Informational RFC from the Internet Architecture Board and continues to guide IETF deliberation and standard-setting toward considering the interests of end users above other stakeholders when there is a conflict.

sections.title: Technical Decisions Are Not Neutral
sections.content:
IETF members often think they are making purely technical decisions based on technical merit. But the running code that results from IETF work has profound effects beyond technology: it defines what is possible on the Internet and who is empowered.

As the Internet increasingly mediates essential functions, it has become political. It has helped people overthrow governments, revolutionize social orders, and control populations. It has created wealth and destroyed it. All of this raises the question: For whom do we go through the pain of gathering consensus and writing running code?
sections.plainLanguage: Making Internet rules is not just math and engineering. It shapes what people can do. So the people making the rules should think about what is fair and good for regular people.

sections.title: Who Are End Users?
sections.content:
In this document, end users are human users whose activities IETF standards support, sometimes indirectly. The end user of a protocol to manage routers is not a router administrator; it is the people using the network that the router operates within.

End users are not a homogenous group. They might have different views about how the Internet should work and occupy several roles: seller, buyer, publisher, reader, service provider, and consumer. An end user might browse the web, videoconference with colleagues, send messages, or perform remote surgery. A person might have many interests—privacy, security, flexibility, reachability—that sometimes conflict.

End users include not only people directly using a system but also indirect users: a child using a browser, a person pictured in a photograph, a person in a room with Internet-connected sensors. These less-direct interactions are harder to evaluate but are still part of the concept of end user.
sections.plainLanguage: End users are the regular people using the Internet: you browsing a website, texting a friend, watching a video. Not companies selling things or governments. Not even the engineers building the network.

sections.title: Why Prioritize End Users?
sections.content:
The Internet technical community has focused on user needs since the very beginning. RFC 1 stated that a goal must be to stimulate easy use by a wide class of users. The IETF mission statement says the Internet exists to help build a better human society. The IETF is explicitly not value-neutral; it wants the Internet to be useful for communities that share its commitment to openness and fairness.

Merely advancing measurable Internet success—size, bandwidth, number of users—is not an adequate goal. Technology is often used as a lever to assert power over users rather than empower them. Prioritizing end users can also help ensure the long-term health of the Internet: perceptions that the IETF has been captured by vendors harm its credibility and its relevance. End users are the driving force behind the network's value. Not prioritizing them jeopardizes the network effect that provides so much value.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet was always meant to be for regular people. And if the people who design it ignore regular people and just do what big companies want, people will stop trusting it and stop using it.

sections.title: How to Prioritize End Users
sections.content:
The IETF can prioritize end users in several ways. First, it should engage the Internet community, not just IETF members. The IETF does not have unique insight into what is good for end users; it should consult with that broader community, especially civil society organizations, by taking the initiative to contact them and explain IETF work. Second, it should create user-focused system designs, as HTTP does with the user agent role. The web browser acts as an intermediary representing end-user interests, allowing multiple implementations and giving users switching power.

Third, the IETF should examine its work for negative impacts on end users and take steps to mitigate them. When a conflict exists between end users and other stakeholders, the IETF should err on the side of protecting end users. Fourth, when end-user needs conflict (such as across jurisdictions), the IETF should design for the worst case: if a user can be harmed somewhere, they probably will be. Finally, the IETF should not prioritize internal convenience—editor convenience, IETF process matters, or architectural purity—over end-user needs.
sections.plainLanguage: Ask real Internet users what they need. Design systems that let users make choices. Check if decisions hurt people. When regular users conflict with big companies, pick the side of users. Do not just make things convenient for engineers.
